lessons.title: What Is DevOps and Why Do Companies Use It?
lessons.metaTitle: What Is DevOps? Lifecycle and Culture
lessons.description: Learn what DevOps means, why companies use it, the DevOps lifecycle and principles, how it differs from Agile and traditional IT, and its culture.

content.text: Picture a restaurant where the cooks and the waiters never talk to each other. The cooks make food and push it through a window. The waiters carry it out and hear all the complaints. When a dish comes back, nobody agrees whose fault it was. Software companies used to work in a very similar way. One group, the developers, wrote the code. A different group, operations, ran the servers. Developers wanted to ship new features quickly. Operations wanted nothing to change, because every change could break the site. The two goals pulled in opposite directions, and releases were slow, stressful and often happened late at night.

DevOps is the name for a different way of working. The word joins two words: development and operations. It is not one tool and it is not one job title. It is a set of habits, practices and tools that help people build, test, release and run software together, in small safe steps, so that changes reach users quickly and do not break things. Some companies have people with the title DevOps Engineer, and this course will teach the skills those people use. But the idea is bigger than a title: the people who build a system also care about how it runs.
Why companies use DevOps

items: **Faster releases.** Instead of one big release every few months, a team can release small changes many times a week, or even many times a day. Small changes are easier to understand and easier to undo.
**Fewer failures.** Automatic tests and repeatable deployments catch mistakes before users see them. A release that is done by a script is done the same way every time.
**Quicker recovery.** When something does break, good monitoring shows it within minutes and a known process brings it back. Teams measure how long this takes and work to make it shorter.
**Less manual work.** Setting up servers by hand, copying files and clicking through consoles is slow and easy to get wrong. DevOps replaces it with code that anyone can read and run.
**Better teamwork.** Developers, testers, security people and operations people share goals and tools, so there is less blaming and more fixing.

content.text: We will not quote percentages or company statistics here. Reports about how much faster DevOps teams are exist, but they differ by survey and year, so read a recent one yourself before you repeat a number to anyone.
The DevOps lifecycle
DevOps is often drawn as a loop, because the work never really ends. The loop has eight steps. You can remember them as a story of one change travelling from an idea to the users and back again.

items: **Plan** what to build or fix, for example in a ticket board.
**Code** the change and keep it in Git.
**Build** the code into something that can run, such as a package or a container image.
**Test** it automatically, so mistakes are found early.
**Release** it: the change is approved and stored, ready to go out.
**Deploy** it to servers or to the cloud.
**Operate** it: keep it running, scale it, back it up.
**Monitor** it: watch errors, speed and cost, and bring what you learn back into the next plan.

content.text: The last step feeds the first one. If monitoring shows that the login page is slow, that becomes a new ticket in Plan. This loop is the heart of DevOps, and every module in this course is one part of it.
The main principles

items: **Automate repeating work.** If you do something by hand twice, think about writing a script for it.
**Small, frequent changes.** A change of ten lines is simple to review and simple to roll back. A change of ten thousand lines is neither.
**Everything in version control.** Not only application code, but also server settings, pipelines and documentation.
**Measure.** You cannot improve what you cannot see, so teams track things like how often they deploy and how often a release fails.
**Shared responsibility.** The team that builds a feature also helps to run it, and learns from its failures without hunting for someone to blame.

content.text: DevOps and Agile

Agile is a way of planning and building software in short cycles, with regular feedback from users. It mostly answers the question: how do we decide what to build and keep the work flexible? DevOps answers a different question: how do we get what we built safely into the hands of users and keep it running? The two fit together well. A team can be Agile in how it plans and DevOps in how it ships. Having one without the other usually leaves a gap, either good plans with slow releases or fast releases of the wrong things.
DevOps and traditional IT

items: **Traditional IT** often has separate teams for development, testing and operations, with hand-overs and approval meetings between them. Releases are big and rare. Servers are set up by hand, so two servers that should be the same slowly become different.
**DevOps** puts these steps into one flow with automation. Releases are small and frequent. Servers are described in code, so a new one can be created in the same way every time.

content.text: This is not a story of good against bad. Big organisations that handle money, health records or government data still need approvals and strict records. DevOps does not remove them. It tries to make them automatic and visible, for example a pipeline that will not deploy until the tests pass and a named person has clicked Approve.
What the culture looks like

Tools are the easy part. The harder part is how people behave. In a healthy DevOps team, people talk about problems early, share what they learn, and write down how things work so that knowledge does not live in one person’s head. When something fails, the team holds a calm review that asks what in the system allowed the mistake, not who made it. This is often called a blameless review, and it only works if managers protect it. If you join a team and find the culture is the opposite, that is useful information too, and you can still use the technical skills in this course.
Your task

items: Write down the last three times software you use broke or changed. For each one, guess which step of the lifecycle failed: plan, code, build, test, release, deploy, operate or monitor.
In your own words, write two sentences: what is DevOps, and why is it not just a tool?
Pick one thing you do by hand often (for example copying files or restarting a program) and write the steps. You will automate something like it in the Linux lessons.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: You can name the eight steps of the lifecycle in order.
You can explain the difference between DevOps and Agile in one or two sentences.
You can give two reasons a company would move from big rare releases to small frequent ones.

steps.say: A change starts as a plan: a ticket or an idea.
It is coded and built into something that can run. The code lives in Git.
Automatic tests and a release step check the change before users ever see it.
The change is deployed and watched. What monitoring shows becomes the next plan, so the loop starts again.

faqs.q: Is DevOps a job or a method?
faqs.a: Both are used. DevOps is mainly a way of working that joins building and running software. Some companies also hire people with the title DevOps Engineer, whose daily work is automation, pipelines, cloud and monitoring.

faqs.q: Do I need to be a programmer to learn DevOps?
faqs.a: You need to be comfortable reading and writing simple scripts and configuration files. You do not need to build large applications. This course teaches the scripting you need from the start.

faqs.q: Does DevOps replace testers and operations staff?
faqs.a: No. It changes how they work together and automates repeating tasks. Testing, security and operations skills are still needed, often inside the same team.

quiz.q: Which best describes DevOps?
options: A set of practices and tools that help people build, test, release and run software together in small safe steps
A job title that only operations staff hold
A single tool that deploys websites

quiz.q: In the DevOps lifecycle, what happens after Monitor?
options: What you learn feeds back into the next Plan

quiz.q: What does a blameless review ask?
options: Whether the team should be smaller
What in the system allowed the mistake

lessons.title: CI, CD, DevSecOps, GitOps and SRE Explained
lessons.metaTitle: CI/CD, DevSecOps, GitOps and SRE Explained
lessons.description: Understand continuous integration, continuous delivery and deployment, DevSecOps, GitOps and Site Reliability Engineering, and how these terms fit together.

content.text: DevOps comes with a lot of short names. They are easy to mix up, and job descriptions use them freely. This lesson gives each one a plain meaning and shows how they connect, so that when you read a job post or an article you know what is being asked. We will use one small running example: a team that keeps a website in Git and wants every change to reach the live site safely.
Continuous Integration (CI)

Integration means putting different people’s work together. In the old way, developers worked alone for weeks and tried to join their code at the end, and the join was painful. Continuous Integration means that everyone adds their work to the shared project often, at least daily, and each time a robot builds the project and runs the tests. If something breaks, the team knows within minutes, while the change is still small and fresh in the author’s mind. The robot is a CI server or a CI service such as GitHub Actions or Jenkins, which you will meet later in this course.
Continuous Delivery and Continuous Deployment
The two CDs are a common source of confusion, because they share the letters CD. They differ in one step.

items: **Continuous Delivery** means every change that passes the tests is automatically prepared so that it could be released at any moment. A person still decides when to press the button.
**Continuous Deployment** goes one step further: every change that passes all checks goes to the live system automatically, with no button.

content.text: Which is better depends on the product and the rules. A small website may use continuous deployment. A bank app may use continuous delivery with a required approval. Both rely on the same foundation: good automatic tests and a deployment that is safe to repeat. When you see CI/CD written together, it usually means the whole path from commit to release.
DevSecOps

Security used to be a checkpoint at the end: a separate team reviewed the finished product, often right before launch, and found problems that were expensive to fix. DevSecOps means building security into every step instead. Typical examples are scanning code for known weak spots, checking that libraries you depend on have no known problems, scanning container images, and keeping passwords and keys out of the code. The idea is called shift left, which means moving checks earlier in the loop, towards the left side of the diagram, where mistakes are cheaper to fix. You will build these checks in the security module.
GitOps

GitOps is a way to run systems where Git is the source of truth. You describe what you want the live system to look like in files in a Git repository, for example which version of the app should run and how many copies. A tool watches the repository and makes the real system match it. To change production you do not log in to a server. You open a pull request, someone reviews it, you merge it, and the tool applies it. This gives you review, a history of every change and an easy way back: revert the commit. Tools that do this for Kubernetes include Argo CD and Flux, which have their own lessons later.
Site Reliability Engineering (SRE)

SRE began at Google as a way of running big systems by treating operations as a software problem. An SRE team writes code to run and fix services, and sets clear targets for how reliable a service must be. Two ideas are worth knowing now. First, you do not aim for perfect reliability, which is impossible and very costly. You agree a target, for example the site should answer correctly 99.9 percent of the time, and that leaves a small allowed amount of failure called an error budget. Second, if the budget is spent, the team slows down new features and focuses on stability. The target numbers in this course are examples only: your own service and your own users decide what is right.
How they fit together

items: A developer pushes a change to Git (GitOps starts here).
CI builds and tests it, including security scans (CI and DevSecOps).
The change is delivered or deployed to the live system (CD).
The system is watched against agreed targets, and the team learns from incidents (SRE).

content.text: None of these needs a particular tool. They are ideas, and you can start small. A single script and a tiny test suite is already a beginning of CI.

Job posts often mix these terms or use them loosely. When you are not sure what a company means, ask in the interview: what does your pipeline do after a commit, and who is on call? The answer tells you more than the job title does.
Your task

items: Draw the path of one change from commit to live site on paper. Mark where tests run, where a person approves and where monitoring sits.
Write one sentence for each term (CI, continuous delivery, continuous deployment, DevSecOps, GitOps, SRE) without looking at the lesson.
Decide which of delivery or deployment a hospital booking system and a personal blog would use, and why.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: You can explain the difference between delivery and deployment.
You can say what shift left means.
You can explain in one sentence why GitOps uses pull requests for production changes.

steps.say: Every change starts in Git. With GitOps, Git also describes the live system.
CI builds the change and runs the tests and security scans on every push.
Continuous delivery prepares the release. Continuous deployment sends it live by itself.
SRE practices watch the service against targets and feed lessons back to the team.

faqs.q: What is the difference between continuous delivery and continuous deployment?
faqs.a: With delivery, a change that passes the checks is ready to release and a person chooses when. With deployment, it goes live automatically after the checks.

faqs.q: Is GitOps only for Kubernetes?
faqs.a: It is most common with Kubernetes, but the idea of keeping the desired state in Git and applying it automatically can be used for other systems too.

faqs.q: Is SRE the same as DevOps?
faqs.a: They overlap. DevOps is a broad set of practices. SRE is a specific way of running services with reliability targets, error budgets and a software approach to operations.

quiz.q: What is the difference between continuous delivery and continuous deployment?
options: Delivery means testing only and deployment means coding only
Delivery leaves the final release to a person; deployment sends passing changes live automatically

quiz.q: What does shift left mean in DevSecOps?
options: Writing code from the left side of the screen
Moving security checks earlier in the process

quiz.q: In GitOps, how do you change production?
options: Log in to a server and edit files by hand
Open a pull request, get it reviewed and merge it, and a tool applies it

lessons.title: DevOps Tools, Architecture and the Engineer’s Role
lessons.description: See the map of DevOps tools by job, a typical architecture from Git to production, what a DevOps engineer does, and a realistic six month learning plan.

content.text: The DevOps tool list looks frightening: hundreds of logos on one poster. The secret is that tools are grouped by the job they do, and each group has a few common choices. You do not need to learn all of them. You need to understand the jobs, learn one tool for each, and know that the others do something similar. This lesson gives you that map, shows how the parts connect in a typical system, and describes what a DevOps engineer actually does in a working week.
The tool map, by job

items: **Version control:** Git, with GitHub, GitLab or Bitbucket to host it.
**Operating system and scripting:** Linux and Bash, sometimes Python.
**CI/CD:** GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Jenkins, Azure Pipelines, AWS CodePipeline.
**Containers:** Docker to package an app, Kubernetes to run many containers.
**Cloud:** AWS, Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud.
**Infrastructure as Code:** Terraform to create cloud resources, Ansible to configure servers.
**Monitoring and logs:** Prometheus, Grafana, the ELK stack, OpenTelemetry, and each cloud’s own tools.
**Security:** secret stores such as HashiCorp Vault, scanners such as Trivy, and the cloud’s identity systems.

content.text: Notice that for every job there is more than one name. Employers differ in what they have chosen. If you understand what a CI tool does, moving from Jenkins to GitHub Actions takes days, not months, because the ideas are the same: a trigger, some jobs, some steps, some secrets.
A typical architecture
Here is a simple, common setup for a web application, from keyboard to user. Real companies add more pieces, but the shape stays similar.

items: A developer pushes code to a **Git repository**.
A **CI pipeline** starts, builds the app, runs tests and scans, and creates a **container image**.
The image is stored in a **registry** (a private shelf for images).
A **deployment** step tells the platform, for example Kubernetes or a cloud service, to run the new image.
The app runs behind a **load balancer** that spreads visitors over several copies and handles HTTPS.
A **database** and storage hold the data, usually managed by the cloud provider.
**Monitoring and logging** collect metrics and messages from every part and send alerts to the team.
All of the cloud pieces are described in **Infrastructure as Code**, so the whole environment can be recreated.

content.text: What a DevOps engineer does
Titles vary: DevOps Engineer, Cloud Engineer, Platform Engineer, Site Reliability Engineer. The daily work overlaps a lot. A typical week may include these tasks.

items: Building and fixing CI/CD pipelines so developers get fast, reliable feedback.
Writing Terraform or Ansible code to create and update servers and cloud services.
Looking after containers and clusters: upgrades, scaling, costs.
Setting up dashboards and alerts, and answering them when they fire, including some on-call duty.
Helping developers with deployment problems and making their work easier.
Reviewing security settings, access rights and backups.
Writing short documents so that others can repeat what you did.

content.text: Salaries, demand and hiring depend on country, company and year, and no course can promise a job. We do not quote figures. What we can say honestly is that these skills are asked for in many job descriptions, and that projects you can show are better evidence than a certificate list.
A realistic learning plan

The syllabus behind this course suggests six months for a beginner who studies a few hours a day. Treat it as a guide, not a deadline. People learn at different speeds, and a full-time job or family changes the numbers.

items: **Month 1:** Linux, networking and Git. These are the base for everything else.
**Month 2:** one cloud provider, for example AWS or Azure. Pick one and go deep, because the ideas transfer.
**Month 3:** Docker and a CI/CD pipeline.
**Month 4:** Kubernetes and Terraform.
**Month 5:** monitoring and DevSecOps.
**Month 6:** bigger projects, a portfolio and, if you want, a certification.

content.text: If you have already built a small website and put it on a server, you are ahead. The best plan is to take that real application and use it as the project all the way through: put it in Git, build a pipeline, containerise it, deploy it to the cloud, describe it in Terraform and add monitoring. One application, improved step by step, teaches more than ten tutorials.
How this course is organised

The lessons follow the order of the learning plan. Linux, networking and Git come first, then cloud basics, then the cloud providers, then Docker, Kubernetes, pipelines, Infrastructure as Code, monitoring, security and reliability, ending with ten projects and an interview question bank. Every lesson ends with a task you do yourself and a way to check that it worked.
Your task

items: Make a table with the eight tool jobs above. For each job write the tool you plan to learn first and one alternative.
Choose a small application of your own (even a static page or a tiny Node app) to use as your project through the whole course.
Block out study time in your calendar for the next four weeks, and write what you will finish each week.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: You can name one tool for each job in the map and say what it does.
You can describe the path of a change from Git to users in about eight steps.
You have chosen the application you will use as your running project.

steps.say: Code and configuration live in a Git repository.
A pipeline builds, tests and scans the change, then produces an image.
The platform in the cloud runs the new version behind a load balancer.
Monitoring collects metrics and logs and alerts the team when something is wrong.

faqs.q: Which cloud should I learn first, AWS, Azure or Google Cloud?
faqs.a: Pick one and learn it well. AWS has the most learning material and many job posts mention it. Azure is common in companies that use Microsoft products. The ideas carry over, so switching later is much easier than the first time.

faqs.q: Do I need a certification to get a DevOps job?
faqs.a: Not always. Some employers value them, others care more about projects and experience. Certifications can give your study a structure, and exam details change, so check the current objectives before you prepare.

faqs.q: Can I learn DevOps without a company server or cloud account?
faqs.a: Yes for many topics. Linux, Git, Docker, scripts and many tools run on your own computer. Cloud providers offer free tiers or trial credits, but the terms change, so read them and set a spending alert before you create anything.

quiz.q: Which tool group is Terraform part of?
What is the best project for learning DevOps across the whole course?
options: One real application improved step by step: Git, pipeline, container, cloud, Terraform, monitoring

quiz.q: Why is it fine to learn one CI tool first?
options: The ideas such as triggers, jobs, steps and secrets carry over to other CI tools
Employers only use one CI tool
All CI tools are identical in every detail

lessons.title: Linux Basics: Distributions, the Terminal and Core Commands
lessons.metaTitle: Linux Basics: Terminal and Core Commands
lessons.description: Learn what Linux is, how it is built, which distribution to choose, how to try it safely, and the terminal commands to move around and manage files.

content.text: Almost every server you will meet in DevOps runs Linux. Cloud virtual machines, containers, build servers and most websites sit on it. That is why this course starts with Linux before any cloud or container tool: if you are comfortable in a Linux terminal, everything later is easier. You do not have to love it. You only need to be able to move around, read files, change things carefully and understand error messages.
What Linux is

Linux is an operating system kernel. The kernel is the core part that talks to the hardware: it decides which program gets the processor, manages memory, reads disks and handles the network. Around the kernel sit tools, libraries and programs. A bundle of the kernel plus those tools is called a distribution, or distro. Linux is free and open source, which means anyone can read, change and share the code, and that is a big reason it spread so widely.
The layers, simply

items: **Hardware:** the processor, memory, disks and network card.
**Kernel:** controls the hardware and gives programs a safe way to use it.
**Shell:** a program that reads the commands you type, for example Bash.
**Programs and services:** everything else, from a text editor to a web server.

content.text: Which distribution

items: **Ubuntu and Debian:** very common on servers and in tutorials. They use the `apt` package tool. Ubuntu Server is a good first choice.
**RHEL, Rocky Linux, AlmaLinux and CentOS Stream:** the Red Hat family, common in large companies. They use `dnf` (older ones use `yum`).
**Amazon Linux:** the default on many AWS machines, in the Red Hat style.

content.text: The commands in this course work on all of them unless the lesson says otherwise. The biggest difference you will notice is the package tool and the exact location of a few files.
Ways to try Linux safely

items: **WSL on Windows:** Windows Subsystem for Linux gives you an Ubuntu terminal inside Windows. It is the quickest start for many learners.
**A virtual machine:** install VirtualBox or similar and run Ubuntu in a window. Mistakes cost nothing, because you can delete the machine.
**A cloud server:** a small virtual machine from a provider. It is real, but remember to switch it off, and set a billing alert.
**macOS:** the terminal is similar to Linux for many commands, though a few tools differ.

content.text: Do not practise destructive commands on your main computer or a company server. Use a practice machine. A single wrong `rm -rf` in the wrong folder can delete real work, and there is no recycle bin.
The terminal and the shell

The terminal is the window. The shell is the program inside it that understands your commands. You type a command, press Enter, and the shell runs it and prints the result. A command has a name, then options that start with a dash, then arguments such as file names. For example, in `ls -l /var/log`, `ls` is the command, `-l` is an option and `/var/log` is the argument.
Commands you will use every day

items: `pwd` shows where you are. `cd folder` moves into a folder, `cd ..` goes up one level, and `cd ~` goes to your home folder.
`ls` lists files. `ls -la` shows details and hidden files (names that start with a dot).
`mkdir name` makes a folder and `mkdir -p a/b/c` makes a whole path.
`cp from to` copies and `mv from to` moves or renames. `cp -r` copies a folder.
`rm file` deletes a file. `rm -r folder` deletes a folder and everything in it. There is no undo.
`cat file` prints a file. `less file` lets you scroll through it, and `q` quits.
`head -n 5 file` and `tail -n 5 file` show the first and last lines. `tail -f file` keeps following new lines, which is perfect for logs.
`grep word file` finds lines that contain a word. `grep -r word folder` searches a whole folder.
`find /path -name "*.log"` finds files by name.
`man command` opens the manual for a command, and `command --help` gives a short summary.

content.text: Paths and the folder map

Linux has one big tree that starts at `/`, called root. A path that starts with `/` is absolute, and works from anywhere. A path that does not is relative to where you are. A few folders matter for DevOps: `/etc` holds configuration, `/var/log` holds logs, `/home` holds users’ files, `/tmp` is for temporary files, `/usr/bin` holds programs and `/opt` is often used for extra software. When something breaks, the answer is very often in a file under `/etc` or `/var/log`.
Work with files, step by step

mkdir -p ~/practice/logs
cd ~/practice
echo "hello devops" > notes.txt
cat notes.txt
cp notes.txt logs/notes-copy.txt
ls -l logs
mv logs/notes-copy.txt logs/old-notes.txt
grep devops logs/old-notes.txt

The `>` sign sends the output of a command into a file instead of the screen, and replaces what was there. `>>` adds to the end instead. The pipe `|` sends the output of one command into another, and you will use it constantly, for example `ls -l | grep log`.
Two habits that save you

items: **Use Tab.** Press Tab to complete file names and commands. It saves typing and catches spelling mistakes.
**Read before you run.** If you paste a command from the internet, read what it does first, especially if it contains `sudo`, `rm` or a pipe into `sh`.

content.text: Your task

items: Set up a practice Linux machine (WSL, a virtual machine or a cloud server).
Run the practice commands above and check each result with `ls` and `cat`.
Use `man ls` to find the option that sorts files by size, and try it.
Use `find` to list all `.conf` files under `/etc`, then use `grep -r` to find which one mentions `localhost`.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: `pwd` shows the folder you expect after each `cd`.
You can create, copy, move, read and delete a file without looking up the commands.
You can say what `/etc` and `/var/log` are for.

steps.say: You type a command in the terminal.
The shell reads it and starts the right program.
The program asks the kernel for what it needs, such as reading a folder.
The kernel talks to the disk and returns the answer, which the shell prints.

faqs.q: Do I need to install Linux as my main system to learn DevOps?
faqs.a: No. WSL on Windows, a virtual machine or a small cloud server is enough. Many people learn this way and keep their normal system.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a distribution and Linux?
faqs.a: Linux is the kernel. A distribution such as Ubuntu bundles the kernel with tools, a package manager and defaults, so you can install and use it.

faqs.q: Is there an undo for rm?
faqs.a: No. The shell does not use a recycle bin. Take care with rm, and for important folders keep backups or use a version control system.

quiz.q: What is the kernel?
options: The core part of the system that talks to hardware, memory and processes

lessons.title: Linux File Permissions, Users and Groups
lessons.description: Understand who owns files in Linux, read rwx permissions and the numbers like 644 and 755, use chmod and chown, and manage users, groups and sudo safely.

content.text: Linux was built for many people to share one machine, so every file has an owner and a set of rules about who may read, change or run it. These rules are the first line of defence on a server. They also cause a large share of the beginner errors you will see, such as Permission denied. If you understand them once, you will fix those errors in seconds, and you will stop reaching for the dangerous shortcut of giving every file full access.
Owner, group and others

Every file has three kinds of people attached to it. The **owner** is usually the user who created it. The **group** is a named set of users. **Others** is everyone else on the system. For each of these three, there are three possible rights.

items: **r (read):** see the contents of a file, or list the names in a folder.
**w (write):** change a file, or add and remove files inside a folder.
**x (execute):** run a file as a program, or enter a folder with `cd`.

content.text: Run `ls -l` and you will see a line like `-rwxr-xr-- 1 asha devs 120 Mar 1 notes.sh`. The first character is the type: a dash for a file, `d` for a folder. The next nine characters are three groups of three: owner `rwx`, group `r-x`, others `r--`. Then come the owner name, the group name, the size, the date and the file name.
The numbers: 644, 755, 600

Each right has a value: read is 4, write is 2 and execute is 1. Add them for each group. So `rwx` is 4 + 2 + 1 = 7, `r-x` is 4 + 1 = 5, `r--` is 4, and `rw-` is 6. A permission of 755 means owner 7, group 5, others 5. You will meet a few numbers again and again.

items: **644** (rw-r--r--): normal files. The owner can edit, everyone can read.
**755** (rwxr-xr-x): programs and scripts, and many folders. Everyone can run, only the owner can edit.
**600** (rw-------): private files such as SSH keys. Only the owner can use them.
**770** (rwxrwx---): a shared folder for a group, with nothing for others.

content.text: A real run

This small script creates a few files in a temporary folder, sets different permissions, and prints the result with `stat`. It was run in the course lab. The script in this lesson was run on Linux in the course lab (bash 5, Python 3.13). The output shown is real. Your numbers (memory, disk, dates) will be different.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# perm-demo.sh - shows how chmod numbers map to rwx. Runs in a temporary folder.
set -euo pipefail
DIR=$(mktemp -d)
cd "$DIR"
touch notes.txt run.sh secret.key
mkdir shared

chmod 644 notes.txt      # owner read+write, everyone else read
chmod 755 run.sh         # owner all, everyone else read+execute
chmod 600 secret.key     # owner read+write, nobody else
chmod 770 shared         # owner and group all, others nothing

stat -c '%a  %A  %n' notes.txt run.sh secret.key shared
cd /
rm -rf "$DIR"

644  -rw-r--r--  notes.txt
755  -rwxr-xr-x  run.sh
600  -rw-------  secret.key
770  drwxrwx---  shared
Changing permissions and owners

chmod 644 notes.txt        # numbers
chmod u+x script.sh        # add execute for the user (owner)
chmod go-w shared.txt      # remove write for group and others
chmod -R 755 site/         # apply to a folder and all inside it
sudo chown asha:devs report.txt   # change owner and group
sudo chown -R www-data:www-data /var/www/site

Letters work too: `u` is the user (owner), `g` the group, `o` others and `a` all. A plus adds a right and a minus removes it. A common beginner mistake is `chmod 777`, which gives everyone full control. It makes the error go away, and leaves the door open. Work out which user needs which right instead. For example, a web server that must read your site files needs read access, not write access.
Users and groups

items: `whoami` shows your user, `id` shows your user number and groups.
`sudo adduser maya` creates a user on Debian and Ubuntu (`useradd` is the lower-level command).
`sudo usermod -aG docker maya` adds Maya to the group called docker. The `-a` is important: without it you replace her other groups.
`sudo passwd maya` sets a password.
`groups maya` lists her groups, and `getent group docker` lists the members of a group.
`sudo deluser maya` removes a user.

content.text: Users and groups are stored in `/etc/passwd` and `/etc/group`. Passwords are not in these files but in `/etc/shadow`, which only the administrator can read.
sudo and the root user

The root user can do anything, including destroy the system. Instead of logging in as root, administrators use `sudo`, which runs one command with root power after checking that you are allowed. Permission to use sudo is set in `/etc/sudoers`, which you edit only with the `visudo` command, because it checks your syntax before saving. If it is wrong, you could lock yourself out. Follow the rule of least privilege: give people the smallest rights that let them do their job.

The demo above runs as a normal shell session. If you run permission experiments as root, you will not see Permission denied, because root ignores the rules. Try them as a normal user to see the errors.
Your task

items: Run the permission demo script and match each number to its letters.
Create a file and use `chmod` to make it readable only by you. Check with `ls -l`.
Create a second user on your practice machine, then try to read your private file as that user and note the error.
Make a folder shared by a group: create the group, add two users, set the folder group and use mode 770.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: You can turn 750 into letters and back without looking it up.
You can explain why chmod 777 is a bad fix.
You can add a user to a group without removing their other groups.

steps.say: The owner of a file has the first set of rights. With mode 755 the owner gets 7: read, write and execute.
The group gets the middle number. Here it is 5: read and execute, but no write.
Everyone else gets the last number, also 5 here.
Together the three numbers give the mode of the file: 755.

faqs.q: What does Permission denied mean?
faqs.a: The user running the command does not have the needed right (read, write or execute) on that file or folder, or on a folder in its path. Check with ls -l and id.

faqs.q: Why does a folder need the x permission?
faqs.a: For a folder, x means you may enter it and reach the files inside. Without x on a folder you cannot cd into it, even if you can list its name.

faqs.q: Should I run everything with sudo?
faqs.a: No. Use sudo only for the commands that need it. Running programs as root makes mistakes and attacks much more damaging.

quiz.q: What does a permission of 644 mean?
options: Owner can read and write; group and others can only read

quiz.q: Why is chmod 777 a poor fix for Permission denied?
options: It gives everyone full control instead of fixing who needs which right

quiz.q: Why use usermod -aG instead of usermod -G to add a group?
options: The -a keeps the user’s other groups
It makes the user an administrator

lessons.title: Processes, Packages, Disk, Memory and Monitoring in Linux
lessons.metaTitle: Linux Processes, Packages, Disk and Memory
lessons.description: Manage running programs, install software with apt, dnf or yum, check disk and memory, and write a small system report script that warns when the disk is full.

content.text: When a server is slow or a site is down, the first questions are always the same. What is running? Is the disk full? Is memory used up? Is something using all the processor? This lesson teaches the commands that answer those questions, and then puts them together into a short script you can reuse. You will also learn how to install and update software with the package manager, which is how almost everything gets onto a Linux server.
Processes

A process is a running program. Every process has a number called a PID. Linux starts a first process when it boots, and every other process is started by another one, so they form a family tree. These are the commands to know.

items: `ps aux` lists all processes with their owner, CPU use, memory use and command.
`ps aux | grep node` finds the processes whose line contains the word node.
`top` shows a live list sorted by CPU use. Press `q` to quit. Many people install `htop`, which is easier to read.

`kill 1234` asks process 1234 to stop politely (it sends the TERM signal). `kill -9 1234` forces it to stop. Use the force version only if the polite one fails, because the program gets no chance to save its work.
`command &` runs a command in the background, `jobs` lists them, and `Ctrl+C` stops the one in front.

content.text: Packages
A package manager downloads, installs, updates and removes software, and takes care of the other packages that software needs. Which one you use depends on the distribution.

# Debian and Ubuntu
sudo apt update              # refresh the list of available packages
sudo apt install nginx       # install
sudo apt upgrade             # update everything installed
sudo apt remove nginx        # remove it

# Red Hat family (Amazon Linux, Rocky, Alma, newer CentOS and RHEL)
sudo dnf install nginx
sudo dnf update
# older systems used: sudo yum install nginx

Always run `apt update` before `apt install` on Debian and Ubuntu, so the list is fresh. Only install software from the official repositories or from a vendor you trust, and read the instructions before adding a new repository or running a script from the internet.
Disk

items: `df -h` shows how full each disk is, in readable sizes. Look at the Use% column.
`du -sh folder` shows how big a folder is. `du -sh * | sort -h` lists the items in the current folder from small to large, which finds the space hogs quickly.
`lsblk` lists disks and partitions.
`mount` and `/etc/fstab` control where disks are attached. Edit `fstab` with great care: a wrong line can stop the machine from booting.

content.text: A full disk is one of the most common causes of strange failures: databases stop, logs cannot be written and uploads fail. Many teams set an alert at about 80 percent. That figure is a habit, not a rule. Choose what suits your system.
Memory

`free -m` shows memory in megabytes. Do not be alarmed if the free number is small. Linux uses spare memory to cache files, which makes things faster, and gives it back when programs need it. The column called available is the better number to watch. If the machine starts using swap (disk used as slow memory) heavily, it will feel very slow.
A small system report script

Here is a script that prints the host, uptime, memory and disk use, and exits with an error when the disk is fuller than a limit that you give. An exit code other than zero is how scripts tell other tools, such as a scheduler or a pipeline, that something is wrong. The script in this lesson was run on Linux in the course lab (bash 5, Python 3.13). The output shown is real. Your numbers (memory, disk, dates) will be different.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# sysinfo.sh - a small health report. Usage: ./sysinfo.sh [disk_warn_percent]
set -euo pipefail
WARN="${1:-80}"

echo "Host:    $(hostname)"
echo "Kernel:  $(uname -sr)"
echo "Uptime:  $(uptime -p 2>/dev/null || uptime)"
echo

echo "Memory (MB):"
free -m | awk 'NR==1 || /^Mem:/'
echo

echo "Disk usage of / :"
USED=$(df -P / | awk 'NR==2 {gsub("%","",$5); print $5}')
echo "  ${USED}% used"
if [ "$USED" -ge "$WARN" ]; then
  echo "  WARNING: more than ${WARN}% full"
  exit 1
fi
echo "  OK (below ${WARN}%)"

$ ./sysinfo.sh 80
Host:    vm
Kernel:  Linux 6.18.44-fc-v378
Uptime:  up 4 minutes

Memory (MB):
               total        used        free      shared  buff/cache   available
Mem:            8022         483        7546          16         211        7539

Disk usage of / :
  34% used
  OK (below 80%)
exit code: 0

$ ./sysinfo.sh 1
Host:    vm
Kernel:  Linux 6.18.44-fc-v378
Uptime:  up 4 minutes

Memory (MB):
               total        used        free      shared  buff/cache   available
Mem:            8022         484        7545          16         211        7538

Disk usage of / :
  34% used
  WARNING: more than 1% full
exit code: 1
The first run used a limit of 80 percent and exited with 0. The second used a limit of 1 percent, which is lower than the real use, so the script printed a warning and exited with 1.
System monitoring in one minute

items: `uptime` shows how long the machine has been up and the load averages for the last 1, 5 and 15 minutes. A load near the number of CPU cores means the machine is busy.
`top` or `htop` for processes, `free -m` for memory, `df -h` for disk.
`journalctl -xe` and the files in `/var/log` for messages about what went wrong. You will use them in the next lesson.

content.text: Your task

items: Run `ps aux`, `top` and `free -m` on your practice machine and write down what is using the most memory.
Install `htop` with your package manager, run it and quit with `q`.
Copy the script, run it with different limits, and check its exit code with `echo $?`.
Use `du -sh * | sort -h` in your home folder to find the biggest item.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: You can find the process ID of a program and stop it.
You can install and remove a package on your system.
You can explain what the available column of free -m tells you.

steps.say: A server is slow or failing. Start with a short checklist instead of guessing.
Check the processor and processes with top or htop. Is one program using it all?
Check memory with free -m, and look at the available column.
Check disk space with df -h. A full disk causes many odd failures.

faqs.q: What is the difference between apt and apt-get?
faqs.a: apt-get is the older tool and apt is the newer, friendlier front end for the same package system. Both work on Debian and Ubuntu. Use apt in a terminal and apt-get in scripts if you like stable behaviour.

faqs.q: Why is my memory almost full but the server is fine?
faqs.a: Linux uses spare memory as a file cache. Look at the available figure instead of free. If available is low and swap is heavily used, you have a real shortage.

faqs.q: Is kill -9 safe?
faqs.a: It stops the process at once, without letting it save or clean up. Try a normal kill first and use -9 only when the program does not respond.

quiz.q: Which command shows how full each disk is?
Which column of free -m is the better number to watch?
What does a script exit code other than 0 tell tools such as a pipeline?

lessons.title: Linux Services, systemd, SSH, Cron Jobs and Logs
lessons.metaTitle: Linux Services, systemd, SSH, Cron and Logs
lessons.description: Run programs as services with systemd and systemctl, log in with SSH keys, schedule work with cron, and read logs with journalctl and /var/log.

content.text: A web server, a database or your Node application should start by itself when the machine boots, restart if it crashes, and run without anyone logged in. On modern Linux, a program called systemd looks after that. In this lesson you will learn how to control services, how to log in to a remote server safely with SSH keys, how to schedule repeating jobs with cron, and where to read the logs when something goes wrong. These four skills are what turn a Linux machine into a server you can trust.

This lesson shows configuration that was written carefully but NOT run on a live server for this course. Test it on a practice machine first, and read your own system’s documentation, because paths and versions differ.
Services and systemd
systemd is the first process on most modern distributions, and it starts and watches all the services. You control it with the `systemctl` command.

systemctl status nginx          # is it running? recent log lines
sudo systemctl start nginx       # start now
sudo systemctl stop nginx        # stop now
sudo systemctl restart nginx     # stop then start
sudo systemctl reload nginx      # re-read config without dropping connections (if supported)
sudo systemctl enable nginx      # start at every boot
sudo systemctl disable nginx     # do not start at boot
systemctl is-active nginx        # prints active or inactive
Two ideas are separate: start means run it now, and enable means run it at boot. Beginners often do one and forget the other. `enable --now` does both together.
Writing your own service

To run your own program as a service, you describe it in a unit file. Here is a unit for a Node application. It runs as a normal user, restarts if it crashes, and reads settings from a file that only the owner can see.

# /etc/systemd/system/jobtracker.service
[Unit]
Description=Job Tracker API
After=network.target

[Service]
Type=simple
User=deploy
WorkingDirectory=/opt/jobtracker
EnvironmentFile=/etc/jobtracker.env
ExecStart=/usr/bin/node server.js
Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=3

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

sudo systemctl daemon-reload            # tell systemd about the new file
sudo systemctl enable --now jobtracker
systemctl status jobtracker
journalctl -u jobtracker -f              # follow its logs
Keep passwords and keys in the `EnvironmentFile`, not in the unit file, and set that file to mode 600 so only its owner can read it.
SSH: logging in to a remote server

SSH gives you a secure terminal on another machine. Passwords can be guessed, so servers should use key pairs. A key pair has a private key, which stays on your computer and is never shared, and a public key, which you place on the server. The server can then check that you hold the private key without it ever travelling over the network.

ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "asha laptop"      # creates ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 and .pub
ssh-copy-id deploy@203.0.113.10              # puts the public key on the server
ssh deploy@203.0.113.10                      # log in with the key
chmod 600 ~/.ssh/id_ed25519                  # the private key must be private

The address 203.0.113.10 is a documentation example, not a real server. A short file called `~/.ssh/config` saves typing, for example a block with `Host jobs`, `HostName 203.0.113.10`, `User deploy` and `IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_ed25519`, after which `ssh jobs` is enough. On the server, hardening usually means turning off password login (`PasswordAuthentication no`) and root login (`PermitRootLogin no`) in `/etc/ssh/sshd_config`, then reloading the `ssh` service. Before you close your current session, open a second one and check that you can still log in, so that a typing mistake does not lock you out.
Cron jobs
Cron runs commands on a schedule. You edit your list of jobs with `crontab -e`. Each line has five time fields, then the command: minute, hour, day of month, month, day of week.

# m  h  dom mon dow  command
30 2  *   *   *    /opt/scripts/backup.sh /var/www /backups 7 >> /var/log/backup.log 2>&1
0  *  *   *   *    /opt/scripts/sysinfo.sh 85 || echo "disk warning" | logger -t sysinfo
*/5 * *   *   *    /opt/scripts/healthcheck.sh 127.0.0.1 3000 /health

items: The first line runs at 02:30 every day. The second runs at the start of every hour. The third runs every five minutes.
Use full paths in cron. Cron has a very small environment, so a command that works in your terminal can fail there.
Send output to a log file with `>> file 2>&1`, otherwise errors vanish.
Check the schedule with a site such as crontab.guru, and make jobs safe to run twice.

content.text: Logs

items: `journalctl -u servicename` shows a service’s logs. Add `-f` to follow, `--since "1 hour ago"` to limit the time, and `-p err` to show only errors.
`/var/log/syslog` (Debian and Ubuntu) or `/var/log/messages` (Red Hat family) hold general messages.
`/var/log/auth.log` or `/var/log/secure` show who logged in and who failed.
`/var/log/nginx/error.log` and `access.log` for a web server.
`tail -f` follows a file, and `grep ERROR file` filters it.

content.text: Logs grow, and a full disk stops servers. The `logrotate` tool is set up on most systems to compress and delete old logs. Check that your own application’s log file is covered.
Your task

items: Install nginx on a practice machine and practise start, stop, enable and status.
Write a unit file for a tiny script or Node app, load it and read its logs with `journalctl -u`.
Create an SSH key pair, put the public key on a practice server and log in without a password.
Add a cron job that appends the date to a file every minute, check it, then remove it.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: `systemctl status` shows your service as active (running).
You can log in with your key and not your password.
Your cron job leaves lines in its log file.

steps.say: When the machine boots, systemd starts every enabled service.
Your service starts from its unit file, running as the user you chose.
If it crashes, systemd restarts it after the delay set by Restart and RestartSec.
Every start and every message is recorded. journalctl -u shows the story.

faqs.q: What is the difference between start and enable?
faqs.a: Start runs the service now. Enable makes it start automatically at every boot. You usually want both, and enable --now does both in one command.

faqs.q: Why is my cron job not running?
faqs.a: Common causes are a wrong time field, a relative path, a missing environment, or no permission to run the script. Use full paths, send the output to a log file and check the cron log.

faqs.q: Is it safe to share my SSH public key?
faqs.a: Yes. The public key is meant to be shared. Never share the private key (the file without .pub).

quiz.q: What is the difference between systemctl start and systemctl enable?
options: Start installs it and enable removes it
Start runs the service now; enable makes it start at every boot

quiz.q: Which cron schedule runs a job every five minutes?
Which SSH key must never be shared?

lessons.title: Bash Scripting for DevOps: Variables, Loops, Backups and Log Checks
lessons.description: Write safe Bash scripts with variables, arguments, if tests, loops and exit codes, and build a backup script and a log summary script that were really run.

content.text: A script is a text file of commands. When you notice that you are typing the same five commands every day, that is a script waiting to be written. Scripts are the glue of DevOps: they back up folders, check that services are alive, prepare servers and run inside pipelines. Bash is the shell on almost every Linux server, so a small amount of Bash goes a long way. This lesson teaches the pieces you need and gives you three working scripts.
The first line and the safety line

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

items: `#!/usr/bin/env bash` tells the system which program should run the file.
`set -e` stops the script when a command fails, instead of carrying on and doing damage.
`set -u` treats an unset variable as an error, which catches typos.
`set -o pipefail` makes a pipeline fail if any part of it fails.

content.text: Save the file, for example as `hello.sh`, make it executable with `chmod +x hello.sh` and run it with `./hello.sh`.
Variables, arguments and quotes

NAME="devops"
echo "Hello, $NAME"
SRC="${1:?give a source folder}"      # first argument, or stop with this message
KEEP="${3:-7}"                         # third argument, default 7
TODAY=$(date +%F)                      # capture the output of a command
echo "Backup for $TODAY"

There must be no spaces around the equals sign when you set a variable. Put variables inside double quotes, as in `"$NAME"`, so that file names with spaces do not break your script. `$1`, `$2` are the arguments and `$#` is how many there are. `$?` is the exit code of the last command: 0 means success and anything else means failure.
Tests and loops

if [ -d "$SRC" ]; then
  echo "folder exists"
elif [ -f "$SRC" ]; then
  echo "it is a file"
else
  echo "not found" >&2      # send the message to the error stream
  exit 2
fi

for f in *.log; do
  echo "checking $f"
done

while read -r line; do
  echo "line: $line"
done < sample.log

items: `-d` tests for a folder, `-f` for a file, `-r` for readable, `-z` for an empty text, and `-eq`, `-lt` and `-ge` compare numbers.
Use `&&` to run the next command only if the first succeeded, and `||` to run it only if it failed.
A function groups steps: `backup() { ... }`, then call it by name.

content.text: Script 1: a backup with a retention rule

This script packs a folder into a dated `.tar.gz` and deletes the oldest backups beyond a number you choose. It was run in the course lab with four backups in a row and a limit of two, and it created four files and removed the two oldest. The script in this lesson was run on Linux in the course lab (bash 5, Python 3.13). The output shown is real. Your numbers (memory, disk, dates) will be different.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# backup.sh - tar a folder into a dated file and keep only the newest N backups.
# Usage: ./backup.sh <source_dir> <backup_dir> [keep]
set -euo pipefail
SRC="${1:?source dir}"; DEST="${2:?backup dir}"; KEEP="${3:-7}"
[ -d "$SRC" ] || { echo "no such folder: $SRC" >&2; exit 2; }
mkdir -p "$DEST"
STAMP=$(date +%Y%m%d-%H%M%S)
FILE="$DEST/$(basename "$SRC")-$STAMP.tar.gz"
tar -czf "$FILE" -C "$(dirname "$SRC")" "$(basename "$SRC")"
echo "created $(basename "$FILE")"
# delete the oldest ones beyond $KEEP (names sort by date)
ls -1 "$DEST"/*.tar.gz | sort | head -n -"$KEEP" | while read -r old; do
  rm -- "$old"; echo "removed $(basename "$old")"
done

$ ./backup.sh /srv/site /srv/backups 2
created site-20261112-022321.tar.gz
created site-20261112-022322.tar.gz
created site-20261112-022323.tar.gz
removed site-20261112-022321.tar.gz
created site-20261112-022324.tar.gz
removed site-20261112-022322.tar.gz

A backup you have never restored is only a hope. After you make one, unpack it somewhere else with `tar -xzf` and check the files. Also copy backups to another machine or storage service, because a backup on the same disk does not help if the disk fails.
Script 2: summarise a log

This script counts log lines by level, shows which service has the most errors and prints the most common error messages, using `awk`, `grep`, `sort` and `uniq`. Here it runs on a small sample file. The log lines are made up.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# logwatch.sh - summarise a log file. Usage: ./logwatch.sh sample.log
set -euo pipefail
FILE="${1:?usage: logwatch.sh <logfile>}"
[ -r "$FILE" ] || { echo "cannot read $FILE" >&2; exit 2; }

echo "Lines by level:"
awk '{print $3}' "$FILE" | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn

echo
echo "Errors by service:"
grep ' ERROR ' "$FILE" | awk '{print $4}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn

echo
echo "Most common error text:"
grep ' ERROR ' "$FILE" | sed 's/^.*ERROR [a-z]* *//' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -3

Lines by level:
      4 INFO
      3 ERROR
      1 WARN

Errors by service:
      2 api
      1 worker

Most common error text:
      1 email failed: connection refused
      1 GET /jobs/99 500 database timeout
      1 GET /jobs/12 500 database timeout
Script 3: a health check you can reuse

This script checks that a TCP port accepts connections and that a web address answers with code 200. It exits with 0 when healthy and 1 when not, so a scheduler or pipeline can act on the result. In the lab it was tested against a small local web server: it printed OK for the home page, FAIL with 404 for a missing page, and FAIL when the server was stopped.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# healthcheck.sh - is a TCP port open, and does a URL answer 200? Exit code 0 = healthy.
# Usage: ./healthcheck.sh <host> <port> [path]
set -uo pipefail
HOST="${1:?host}"; PORT="${2:?port}"; PATH_="${3:-/}"

if ! (exec 3<>"/dev/tcp/$HOST/$PORT") 2>/dev/null; then
  echo "FAIL: $HOST:$PORT is not accepting connections"; exit 1
fi
CODE=$(curl -s -o /dev/null -m 3 -w '%{http_code}' "http://$HOST:$PORT$PATH_" || true)
if [ "$CODE" = "200" ]; then
  echo "OK: $HOST:$PORT$PATH_ answered 200"; exit 0
fi
echo "FAIL: $HOST:$PORT$PATH_ answered ${CODE:-nothing}"; exit 1

$ ./healthcheck.sh 127.0.0.1 8765 /
OK: 127.0.0.1:8765/ answered 200
$ ./healthcheck.sh 127.0.0.1 8765 /missing
FAIL: 127.0.0.1:8765/missing answered 404
$ ./healthcheck.sh 127.0.0.1 8765        # server stopped
FAIL: 127.0.0.1:8765 is not accepting connections
Good habits

items: Test scripts on copies of data, not on the real thing. Run `bash -n script.sh` to check the syntax without running it, and `bash -x script.sh` to see each command as it runs.
Never put passwords in a script. Read them from the environment or a protected file.
Make scripts safe to run twice (idempotent), because schedulers and people run things again.
Write a usage line at the top, and print clear messages. Future you will not remember.

content.text: Your task

items: Type the backup script, run it on a folder of test files, and check that old backups are removed.
Run the log script on your own application log, then change it to also show the most active hour.
Use the health check against your own site or a local server, and print its exit code with `echo $?`.
Write a script of your own that automates something you do by hand every day.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: Your scripts stop with a clear message when an argument is missing.
`bash -n` reports no syntax errors for each script.
You restored a backup into a different folder and the files match.

steps.say: A scheduler such as cron, or a pipeline step, starts the script.
The script does its work: a backup, a log check or a health check.
It finishes with an exit code. Zero means success and anything else means failure.
Tools read the code. A pipeline stops on failure, and an alert can be sent.

faqs.q: Should I learn Bash or Python for DevOps?
faqs.a: Learn both over time. Bash is best for short glue tasks on Linux. Python suits longer logic, data handling and working with cloud APIs. This course uses Bash first and Python where it helps.

faqs.q: What does set -euo pipefail do?
faqs.a: It makes the script stop on the first failing command, on an unset variable and on a failed part of a pipe. It turns silent mistakes into clear errors.

faqs.q: Why do my scripts fail in cron but work in my terminal?
faqs.a: Cron runs with a minimal environment and a short PATH. Use full paths to commands and files and redirect output to a log file to see the error.

quiz.q: What does set -e do in a Bash script?
options: Stops the script when a command fails

quiz.q: Why should you quote variables, as in "$NAME"?
options: So file names with spaces do not break the script

quiz.q: Why check that a backup can be restored?
options: A backup that has never been restored is only a hope

lessons.title: Networking Basics: OSI, TCP/IP and IP Addresses
lessons.description: Understand how computers talk over a network: the OSI and TCP/IP models, IPv4 and IPv6, public and private IPs, and how a browser reaches a server.

content.text: Every cloud service, container and website you will work with depends on a network. When a deployment fails with connection refused or timed out, you need to know where to look. Networking looks like a wall of strange letters at first, but the ideas are simple, and you can learn the useful part in a few lessons. This first one gives you the map: how data travels, what the layer models mean and what an IP address is.
What a network is

A network is a group of devices that can send data to each other. Your phone and laptop on home Wi-Fi are on a small network. The internet is a huge number of networks joined together. Data is cut into small pieces called packets. Each packet carries the address it is going to, the address it came from and a piece of the message. The network delivers packets, often by different routes, and the receiving device puts them back in order.
The OSI model: seven layers

To keep this manageable, network engineers describe the work in layers. Each layer does one job and relies on the layer below. The OSI model has seven layers. You do not need to memorise it for daily work, but interviewers like it, and it helps you to say where a problem is.

items: **Physical:** cables, radio signals, the bits on the wire.
**Data link:** moves data between devices on the same local network, using MAC addresses (the fixed hardware address of a network card). Switches work here.
**Network:** moves packets between networks using IP addresses. Routers work here.
**Transport:** manages the conversation between two programs: TCP (reliable) or UDP (fast). Ports live here.
**Session:** keeps a conversation open.
**Presentation:** formats and encrypts the data, for example TLS.
**Application:** the protocols programs speak: HTTP, DNS, SSH, SMTP.

content.text: A useful way to remember the order is the phrase from the bottom: Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away. People like silly phrases, and any phrase that helps you is fine.
The TCP/IP model: four layers
The internet itself uses a simpler model with four layers. It is the one you will see in real life.

items: **Link:** the local network (Wi-Fi, Ethernet).
**Internet:** IP addresses and routing.
**Transport:** TCP and UDP, with ports.
**Application:** HTTP, HTTPS, DNS, SSH and so on.

content.text: OSI layers 5, 6 and 7 are all one Application layer in TCP/IP. In practice, when someone says layer 4 they mean transport, TCP and ports. When they say layer 7 they mean the application, for example HTTP. You will hear these terms when load balancers are described: a layer 4 load balancer looks only at addresses and ports, and a layer 7 load balancer can read the web request.
IP addresses
An IP address identifies a device on a network, like a house number in a street. There are two versions.

items: **IPv4** has four numbers from 0 to 255 separated by dots, for example `192.168.1.25`. It has about 4.3 billion possible addresses, which are no longer enough for all devices.
**IPv6** has much longer addresses written in hexadecimal with colons, for example `2001:db8::1`. It has a gigantic number of addresses. Many networks run both at once.

content.text: Public and private IP addresses

A public IP address can be reached from the whole internet and is unique. Private addresses are for use inside a home, office or cloud network only. Many networks can reuse the same private addresses, because those addresses are never routed over the open internet. Three ranges are reserved for private use in IPv4.

Your laptop probably has a private address such as 192.168.1.25. Your router has one public address, and translates between the two, using a technique called NAT that you will meet in a later lesson. Cloud networks use private ranges too, which is why you will choose ranges like 10.0.0.0/16 when you build a network in AWS.

The addresses in these lessons, such as 192.168.1.25 and 203.0.113.10, are examples. Addresses beginning 203.0.113, 198.51.100 and 192.0.2 are reserved for documentation, so they are safe to use in examples.
What happens when you open a web page

items: Your browser asks DNS for the IP address of the site name.
It opens a TCP connection to that address on port 443 (HTTPS).
TLS starts: the browser and the server agree on keys, and the browser checks the server’s certificate.
The browser sends an HTTP request: GET this page.
The server sends back the page, and the browser shows it.

content.text: Each of these steps can fail, and each failure looks different. A wrong name gives a DNS error. A closed port or a firewall gives connection refused or a timeout. A bad certificate gives a security warning. A broken application gives an error code such as 500. When you troubleshoot, work through the steps in order, and you will find the broken one.
Your task

items: Find your computer’s private IP (`hostname -I` on Linux, `ipconfig` on Windows) and decide which private range it belongs to.
Search for "what is my IP" in a browser and compare the public address with your private one.
Write the five steps of opening a web page from memory, and name the layer of each.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: You can explain the difference between a public and a private IP.
You can name what each of the four TCP/IP layers does.
You can say which step failed if a page shows a certificate warning.

animation.title: A web request, step by step

steps.say: You type a site name in the browser.
The browser asks DNS for the IP address behind that name.
It opens a TCP connection to that address and starts TLS to make it secure.
The server receives the HTTP request and sends back the page.

faqs.q: Do I need to memorise the OSI model?
faqs.a: Not for daily work, but you should know the main layers and where common tools sit: switches at layer 2, routers at layer 3, TCP and UDP at layer 4, HTTP and DNS at layer 7. Interviews often ask.

faqs.q: Why are private IP addresses needed?
faqs.a: There are not enough IPv4 addresses for every device. Private ranges can be reused inside many separate networks, and NAT lets those devices reach the internet through a public address.

faqs.q: Is IPv6 replacing IPv4?
faqs.a: IPv6 adoption keeps growing, and many networks use both. IPv4 is still widespread, so you must understand it, and you should learn IPv6 basics too.

quiz.q: Which OSI layer do routers work at?
Which address range is private?
A browser shows a certificate warning. Which step of opening a page failed?

lessons.title: Subnetting and CIDR Notation Made Simple
lessons.description: Learn what a subnet mask is, read CIDR notation like /24 and /16, count usable addresses, split a network into subnets and check it with Python.

content.text: When you build a cloud network, the first thing it asks is a range such as 10.0.0.0/16, and then a range for each subnet inside it. People find subnetting scary because of the binary maths in old textbooks. You can do the practical part with one idea and one small table, and you can check every answer with a short Python script. By the end of this lesson you will be able to read /24, size a network and split it into parts.
What a subnet is

A subnet is a smaller network cut from a bigger one. Splitting a network has real benefits. Traffic stays inside its own part, you can apply different security rules to each part (for example one subnet for public web servers and another for private databases), and addresses are organised. In AWS, Azure and Google Cloud, this is exactly how you separate public and private resources.
The subnet mask and CIDR
An IPv4 address has 32 bits. Part of it identifies the network and the rest identifies the device inside that network. The subnet mask tells you where the split is. You will see it written two ways.

items: As a dotted mask: `255.255.255.0`.
As CIDR notation (Classless Inter-Domain Routing): a slash and a number, `/24`. The number is how many bits belong to the network.

content.text: So `192.168.1.0/24` means: the first 24 bits (the first three numbers) are the network, and the last 8 bits are for devices. 8 bits give 2 to the power of 8 = 256 addresses. The more bits for the network, the fewer for devices, so a bigger slash number means a smaller network.
The one table you need

items: **/16** = 65,536 addresses. Mask 255.255.0.0. A common size for a whole cloud network.
**/24** = 256 addresses. Mask 255.255.255.0. A common size for a subnet.
**/25** = 128 addresses.
**/26** = 64 addresses.
**/27** = 32 addresses.
**/28** = 16 addresses.
**/30** = 4 addresses, used for links between two devices.
**/32** = 1 address, a single host.

content.text: The pattern: each time the slash number goes up by one, the number of addresses halves. The size is always 2 to the power of (32 minus the slash number).
Usable hosts

In a normal network, the first address is the network address (the name of the network itself) and the last is the broadcast address (to talk to everyone). Neither can be given to a device. So usable hosts equal total addresses minus 2. A /24 gives 254 usable addresses. Cloud providers reserve a few more in each subnet for their own use, which means a /24 subnet in AWS gives fewer than 254. Always check your provider’s documentation before you size a subnet tightly.
Check it with Python

Python has the `ipaddress` module in its standard library, which does the maths for you. This small script prints the details of any network and splits it into smaller ones. The script in this lesson was run on Linux in the course lab (bash 5, Python 3.13). The output shown is real. Your numbers (memory, disk, dates) will be different.

"""subnet.py - answer the usual CIDR questions with Python's standard library."""
import ipaddress, sys

net = ipaddress.ip_network(sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else "10.0.0.0/24")
print(f"Network:      {net.network_address}/{net.prefixlen}")
print(f"Netmask:      {net.netmask}")
print(f"Broadcast:    {net.broadcast_address}")
hosts = list(net.hosts())
print(f"Addresses:    {net.num_addresses}")
print(f"Usable hosts: {len(hosts)}  ({hosts[0]} to {hosts[-1]})" if hosts else "Usable hosts: 0")
print(f"Private:      {net.is_private}")

if net.prefixlen < 30:
    new_prefix = min(net.prefixlen + 2, 30)
    print(f"\nSplit into /{new_prefix} subnets:")
    for s in net.subnets(new_prefix=new_prefix):
        print(f"  {s}")
Splitting a network on paper

Say you have 10.0.0.0/24 and need four equal subnets. Four is 2 squared, so you add two bits to the network part: /24 becomes /26. Each /26 has 64 addresses, so the subnets start at 0, 64, 128 and 192: 10.0.0.0/26, 10.0.0.64/26, 10.0.0.128/26 and 10.0.0.192/26. That matches the output above. To check that an address belongs to a subnet, see whether it lies between the first and last address of the range.
Planning a cloud network

items: Choose a private range for the whole network that does not overlap other networks you may join later, for example 10.0.0.0/16. Overlaps make it impossible to connect two networks.
Split it into subnets by role: public, private application, and private database. Make one set in each availability zone.
Give each subnet enough room to grow, but do not waste the whole range. A /24 or /20 is a common choice for a subnet.
Write the plan in a table before you create anything.

content.text: Subnetting tests in interviews are often about simple cases like these. Practise by splitting a /24 into /26 and /27 subnets by hand, then check with the script.
Your task

items: Run the script on three networks of your choice (for example 172.16.0.0/20 and 10.1.0.0/22) and write down the number of usable hosts.
Plan a network: 10.0.0.0/16 with a public and a private subnet in two availability zones, using /24 subnets. List the four ranges.
Predict, then check, how many addresses a /27 has.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: You can say how many addresses a /26 has without a calculator.
You can explain why usable hosts are two fewer than the total.
Your four subnet ranges do not overlap.

steps.say: You start with one network: 10.0.0.0/24 holds 256 addresses.
Adding two bits to the network part makes it /26. The first subnet holds 64 addresses, from 10.0.0.0.
The next subnet starts 64 higher, at 10.0.0.64.
The last two start at 10.0.0.128 and 10.0.0.192. Together the four use the whole /24.

faqs.q: What does /24 mean?
faqs.a: The first 24 of the 32 bits of the address identify the network. The remaining 8 bits are for devices, which gives 256 addresses.

faqs.q: Why do cloud subnets have fewer usable addresses?
faqs.a: Providers reserve a few addresses in every subnet for their own services such as the router and DNS. The exact number depends on the provider, so check its documentation.

faqs.q: Do I need to do subnetting in binary?
faqs.a: Understanding binary helps, but for daily DevOps work the table of sizes and a tool such as Python’s ipaddress module are enough.

quiz.q: How many addresses does a /24 network have?
A /24 is split into four equal subnets. What size is each?
Why are usable hosts two fewer than the total in a normal network?
options: The first is the network address and the last is the broadcast address

lessons.title: DNS, DHCP, HTTP and HTTPS, TCP and UDP, and Ports
lessons.metaTitle: DNS, DHCP, HTTP, TCP, UDP and Ports
lessons.description: Learn what DNS and DHCP do, how HTTP and HTTPS requests and status codes work, TCP versus UDP, and the common ports a DevOps engineer should know.

content.text: In the last two lessons you learned addresses and networks. Now come the services that make a network usable for people: DNS turns names into addresses, DHCP hands out addresses automatically, HTTP and HTTPS carry web pages, and TCP, UDP and ports decide which program on a machine receives which data. Each one shows up in daily DevOps work, especially when something fails and you must find out why.
DNS: the phone book of the internet

People remember names such as example.com. Computers use IP addresses. DNS (Domain Name System) translates one into the other. When you ask for a name, your computer asks a resolver, usually run by your internet provider or a public service. The resolver asks the system of servers that hold the answer, and keeps the reply for a time (the TTL, time to live) so it does not have to ask again. The records you will meet most often are these.

items: **A:** a name to an IPv4 address. **AAAA:** a name to an IPv6 address.
**CNAME:** a name that is an alias of another name.
**MX:** which servers receive email for the domain.
**TXT:** free text, used for domain verification and email security settings.
**NS:** which servers are in charge of the domain.

content.text: When you change a DNS record, old answers stay in caches until the TTL runs out, so changes can take minutes or hours to be seen everywhere. That is called propagation, and it is a common reason for the answer: I changed it, but I still see the old site. Before a planned move, lower the TTL a day ahead. Tools such as `dig example.com` and `nslookup example.com` show what DNS answers. They are not installed in every container image, so you may need to install them.
DHCP: addresses on request

When your phone joins Wi-Fi, nobody types an address in. DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) on the router gives the device an address, the subnet mask, the gateway (the way out to other networks) and the DNS server, for a limited time called a lease. Servers usually need a fixed address instead, so they get a static address or a reservation, and cloud providers handle this for you. If a device shows an address starting with 169.254, it did not get an answer from a DHCP server.
HTTP and HTTPS

HTTP is the language of the web. The client sends a request with a method, a path and headers, and the server sends back a status code, headers and a body. HTTPS is the same conversation inside TLS, which encrypts it and proves the server’s identity with a certificate.

items: **Methods:** `GET` reads, `POST` creates, `PUT` or `PATCH` changes, `DELETE` removes.
**2xx** success: `200 OK`, `201 Created`.
**3xx** redirect: `301` moved for good, `302` moved for now.
**4xx** the client did something wrong: `400` bad request, `401` not logged in, `403` not allowed, `404` not found, `429` too many requests.
**5xx** the server failed: `500` internal error, `502` bad gateway, `503` unavailable, `504` gateway timeout.

content.text: In DevOps you will see 502, 503 and 504 often. They usually mean a proxy or load balancer could not get a good answer from the application behind it: the app is down, overloaded or slow. Try `curl -I https://example.com` to see the status line and headers, and `curl -v` for the full conversation.
TCP and UDP

items: **TCP** sets up a connection first (the three-way handshake), numbers every piece of data, resends lost pieces and delivers in order. It is reliable and a little slower. Web, email, SSH and databases use it.
**UDP** just sends. There is no connection and no resend. It is fast and light, and fine when old data is useless anyway: video calls, games, DNS lookups.

content.text: Ports

An IP address finds the machine. A port number finds the program on that machine, so one server can run a web server and a database at the same time. Ports go from 0 to 65535. A program listens on a port, and a client connects to it. These are the ones worth knowing by heart.

items: **25 / 587** email sending (SMTP)
**80** HTTP and **443** HTTPS
**3306** MySQL, **5432** PostgreSQL, **27017** MongoDB, **6379** Redis
**3000, 5000, 8080** common for development web apps

content.text: To see what is listening on a Linux machine, use `ss -tlnp` (or `netstat -tlnp` on older systems), which shows the open TCP ports and the program for each. If your app says address already in use, another program holds the port. To test whether you can reach a port from another machine, use `curl` for web services, or the check in the health script of the Linux course.

A service that listens on 127.0.0.1 can only be reached from the same machine. To accept connections from outside, it must listen on 0.0.0.0 (all addresses) or a specific address, and the firewall must allow the port. Mixing these up is the cause of many connection refused problems when a deployment is first set up.
Your task

items: Use `curl -I` on three sites and write down each status code and the `server` header, if shown.
Run `curl -v https://example.com` and find the steps of the TLS handshake and the request in the output.
Install `dnsutils` (Debian and Ubuntu) or `bind-utils` (Red Hat family), run `dig` on a domain and read the A record and TTL.
Start a small local web server, find its port with `ss -tlnp` and connect to it with `curl`.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: You can explain what a 502 and a 404 mean and who is at fault in each case.
You can say why a DNS change is not seen at once.
You can match each of the ports above to its service.

steps.say: A client wants example.com. It does not know the IP address yet.
DNS answers with an A record, and the answer is cached for the TTL.
