The client connects to the web port, 443, over TCP, and TLS secures the connection.
The application answers with a status code. 200 is success, 5xx means the server failed.

faqs.q: Why do I still see the old site after I changed DNS?
faqs.a: DNS answers are cached until their TTL expires, on resolvers and sometimes on your own computer or browser. Wait for the TTL, or lower the TTL before the change next time.

faqs.q: What is the difference between 502 and 504?
faqs.a: A 502 means the proxy got a bad answer from the application behind it. A 504 means the proxy waited and got no answer in time. Both point to a problem behind the proxy.

faqs.q: Why is DNS usually UDP and not TCP?
faqs.a: DNS questions and answers are small, so a fast UDP message is enough. DNS falls back to TCP for large answers.

quiz.q: What does a 502 status code usually point to?
options: A problem behind the proxy or load balancer
The user is not logged in

quiz.q: Why can a DNS change take time to be seen everywhere?
options: Old answers stay cached until the TTL runs out

quiz.q: Which port is HTTPS by default?

lessons.title: Firewalls, NAT, VPN, Load Balancers, TLS and Network Troubleshooting
lessons.metaTitle: Firewalls, NAT, VPN, Load Balancers, TLS
lessons.description: Understand firewalls and ufw, NAT, VPNs, load balancers, reverse proxies, TLS certificates and CDNs, then follow a simple network troubleshooting method.

content.text: This lesson joins the pieces that sit between a visitor and your application: the firewall that decides what may pass, NAT that lets private machines reach the internet, VPNs that connect networks safely, load balancers and reverse proxies that share the work, TLS that encrypts it, and the CDN that puts copies near the visitor. Then it ends with a simple method for finding network problems. Every cloud lesson later uses these ideas under different names.
Firewalls

A firewall allows or blocks traffic using rules. A rule usually names a direction (in or out), a protocol, a port and a source or destination address. The safest approach is to block everything by default and open only what you need. On Ubuntu, the simple tool is `ufw`.

sudo ufw default deny incoming
sudo ufw default allow outgoing
sudo ufw allow 22/tcp        # SSH: allow this BEFORE you enable the firewall
sudo ufw allow 80/tcp
sudo ufw allow 443/tcp
sudo ufw enable
sudo ufw status verbose

The Red Hat family uses `firewalld` with `firewall-cmd`, and underneath both are built on the kernel feature called nftables or iptables. Cloud providers add their own firewalls at the network edge, called security groups and network ACLs in AWS. A request must pass every firewall on its path, so if a port is open in `ufw` but blocked in the cloud security group, it is still blocked. Always check both. This commands block was not run for this course. Be very careful with remote servers: if you enable a firewall without allowing SSH first, you lock yourself out.
NAT

NAT (Network Address Translation) lets many devices with private addresses share one public address. When a private machine opens a connection to the internet, the NAT device swaps the private source address for its own public one, remembers the conversation, and swaps back when the answer returns. Outside machines cannot start a connection to the private machine, which is a handy side effect. In the cloud, a NAT gateway gives private servers a way out (for updates, for example) without giving them a public address.
VPN

A VPN (Virtual Private Network) creates an encrypted tunnel across the internet. A site-to-site VPN joins two networks, for example an office and a cloud network, so they behave like one network. A remote-access VPN lets one person connect to a private network from home. Tools you will meet include WireGuard and OpenVPN, and every big cloud has managed VPN services. A VPN protects the traffic in the tunnel. It does not make a weak server safe.
Load balancers and reverse proxies

items: A **reverse proxy** sits in front of one or more servers and forwards requests to them. Nginx is the common example. It can serve static files, terminate TLS, compress, cache and hide the real servers.

A **load balancer** spreads requests over several copies of an application, and stops sending to a copy that fails its health check. Common ways to pick a server are round robin (take turns) and least connections.
**Layer 4** balancers work with addresses and ports only. **Layer 7** balancers read the HTTP request and can route by path or host name, for example /api to one group and /blog to another.

content.text: A load balancer is what makes a web service both scalable (add more copies) and available (a failed copy is skipped). It needs a health check endpoint in your app, such as /health, that answers 200 only when the app is truly working. The health check script from the Bash lesson is a tiny version of what a load balancer does every few seconds.
TLS and certificates

TLS encrypts the connection and proves who the server is. A certificate says: this public key belongs to this domain, signed by an authority your browser trusts. Certificates expire, and an expired one gives every visitor a scary warning, so renewal must be automatic. Let’s Encrypt is a free authority that issues certificates through the ACME protocol, and tools like Certbot automate it. Cloud providers offer managed certificates that renew by themselves. You can look at a server’s certificate with `openssl s_client -connect example.com:443` or with `curl -vI https://example.com`, and the expiry date is in the output.
Routing, switching and CDN

items: A **switch** connects devices inside one network. A **router** connects different networks and decides the next hop for each packet using a routing table. The default route (0.0.0.0/0) means: for anything I do not know, send it this way, normally to the internet gateway.

A **CDN** (content delivery network) keeps copies of your files on servers in many places, so visitors get them from a nearby server. This makes pages load faster, takes load off your server and can absorb some attacks. It works best for images, scripts and pages that do not change per user.

content.text: A troubleshooting method
When something cannot connect, do not guess. Go from the bottom up and from near to far, and change only one thing at a time.

items: **Is the name right?** Check DNS with `dig` or `nslookup`.
**Can I reach the machine?** Try `ping` (some networks block it, so a failed ping is not proof).
**Is the port open?** Test from the client with the health script, `curl` or `nc -vz host port`.
**Is the service listening?** On the server, `ss -tlnp` shows what listens and on which address.
**Is a firewall in the way?** Check the local firewall, the cloud security group and any network ACL.
**Does the application answer?** Use `curl -v` and read the status code. Then read the application logs.

content.text: This small script is the port and URL test from the Bash lesson. It tells you at once whether the failure is at the port (nothing is listening or a firewall drops it) or in the application (a status code other than 200). It was run in the course lab against a local test server. The script in this lesson was run on Linux in the course lab (bash 5, Python 3.13). The output shown is real. Your numbers (memory, disk, dates) will be different.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# healthcheck.sh - is a TCP port open, and does a URL answer 200? Exit code 0 = healthy.
# Usage: ./healthcheck.sh <host> <port> [path]
set -uo pipefail
HOST="${1:?host}"; PORT="${2:?port}"; PATH_="${3:-/}"

if ! (exec 3<>"/dev/tcp/$HOST/$PORT") 2>/dev/null; then
  echo "FAIL: $HOST:$PORT is not accepting connections"; exit 1
fi
CODE=$(curl -s -o /dev/null -m 3 -w '%{http_code}' "http://$HOST:$PORT$PATH_" || true)
if [ "$CODE" = "200" ]; then
  echo "OK: $HOST:$PORT$PATH_ answered 200"; exit 0
fi
echo "FAIL: $HOST:$PORT$PATH_ answered ${CODE:-nothing}"; exit 1

$ ./healthcheck.sh 127.0.0.1 8765 /
OK: 127.0.0.1:8765/ answered 200
$ ./healthcheck.sh 127.0.0.1 8765 /missing
FAIL: 127.0.0.1:8765/missing answered 404
$ ./healthcheck.sh 127.0.0.1 8765
FAIL: 127.0.0.1:8765 is not accepting connections
Your task

items: On a practice machine, start a simple web server (for example `python3 -m http.server 8000`) and test it with the health script, then stop it and test again.
Draw the path of a request from a visitor to a private application server through a CDN, a load balancer and a firewall.
Look at the certificate of a site you use and find its expiry date.
Write the six troubleshooting steps on a card and use them the next time something does not connect.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: You can explain what NAT does and why a private server cannot be reached from the internet directly.
You can say the difference between a reverse proxy and a load balancer.
Your health check shows the three different results when you test OK, 404 and a stopped server.

steps.say: A visitor requests your site over HTTPS.
A CDN may answer from a nearby copy. Firewall rules decide what traffic is allowed through.
The load balancer picks a healthy copy of the application, and skips any that fail the health check.
The application servers live in a private network and answer through the load balancer.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a firewall and a security group?
faqs.a: A security group is a firewall that the cloud provider applies to your virtual machines. The idea is the same: rules about allowed traffic. In AWS, security groups remember connections, while network ACLs do not.

faqs.q: Can a failed ping prove a server is down?
faqs.a: No. Many networks and servers block ping on purpose. Test the real service on its real port instead.

faqs.q: How do I stop certificates from expiring?
faqs.a: Use automatic renewal: Certbot or another ACME client, or a managed certificate from your cloud provider. Add a monitoring alert for the expiry date as a second safety net.

quiz.q: What is the safest default firewall approach?
options: Block everything and open only what is needed
Open everything and block what is dangerous

quiz.q: What does NAT let many private machines do?
options: Share one public address to reach the internet

quiz.q: In which order should you troubleshoot a connection problem?
options: Name, reachability, port, listening service, firewalls, application

lessons.title: Git for DevOps Teams: Branches, Rebase, Stash, Tags and Pull Requests
lessons.metaTitle: Git for DevOps: Branching and Reviews
lessons.description: Use Git the way DevOps teams do: branching strategies, merge or rebase, stash, reset and revert, cherry-pick, tags for releases, pull requests and code reviews.

content.text: If you already know the basic Git commands, this lesson shows how teams use them to ship software safely. If you are new to Git, first read the free [Git and GitHub course](/learn/git-and-github-course) on this site, then come back, because this lesson assumes you can commit, branch and push. In DevOps, Git is not just where code lives. Pipelines start from it, releases are marked in it, and in GitOps even the live system is described in it. A few habits make that smooth.
Branching strategies
A branching strategy is the team’s agreement about which branches exist and how work flows between them. Three are common.

items: **Trunk-based development:** everyone works in very short branches (a day or two) and merges into `main` often. It relies on good automatic tests and, often, feature flags to hide unfinished work. It suits teams that deploy many times a day.
**GitHub flow:** `main` is always deployable. For every change you create a branch, open a pull request, get a review and tests, merge, and deploy. Simple and very popular.
**Git flow:** long-lived `develop` and `main` branches plus feature, release and hotfix branches. It fits software with scheduled releases and several supported versions, but it has more overhead.

content.text: There is no single best choice. For a small team with a web application, GitHub flow is a good start. Whatever you choose, keep branches short-lived: the longer a branch lives, the harder the merge.
Merge or rebase

Both combine work from two branches. A merge adds a new commit that joins the two histories, and keeps everything as it happened. A rebase replays your commits on top of the latest `main`, which gives a straight line of history that is easier to read. The golden rule of rebase: never rebase commits that other people have already pulled, because you rewrite history and cause trouble for them. A safe pattern is to rebase your own private branch on `main` before you open the pull request, and to merge (or squash) when the pull request is accepted.

git switch -c feature/health-endpoint    # start a branch
git add . && git commit -m "Add /health endpoint"
git fetch origin
git rebase origin/main                     # replay my work on the newest main
git push --force-with-lease -u origin feature/health-endpoint
`--force-with-lease` is a safer force push: it refuses if someone else pushed to your branch in the meantime. You need a force push after a rebase, because history changed.
Stash, reset and revert

items: `git stash` puts your unfinished changes on a shelf so you can switch branches with a clean folder. `git stash pop` brings them back, and `git stash list` shows the shelf.

`git restore file` throws away changes to a file that you have not committed. `git reset --soft HEAD~1` undoes the last commit but keeps the changes ready to commit again. `git reset --hard` destroys uncommitted work, so think before you use it.
`git revert <commit>` makes a new commit that undoes an old one. Use revert, not reset, to undo something that is already shared, because it keeps the history honest.

content.text: Cherry-pick

`git cherry-pick <commit>` copies one commit onto the branch you are on. DevOps teams use it when a fix made on `main` must also go onto a release branch, without taking all the other changes. Prefer small, focused commits, because cherry-picking a commit that mixes five things is painful.
Tags and releases

A tag is a fixed name for one commit, normally used to mark a release such as `v1.4.0`. Pipelines can start a release build when a tag is pushed, and rolling back means deploying the previous tag. A common numbering scheme is semantic versioning: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH, where a patch fixes bugs, a minor adds features without breaking things, and a major may break things.

git tag -a v1.4.0 -m "Release 1.4.0"
git push origin v1.4.0
git tag --list "v1.*"
Pull requests and code review

A pull request (PR) asks for your branch to be merged and gives others the chance to look first. Good PRs are small, have a clear title and description (what changed and why, and how you tested it) and link to the ticket. Good reviews are kind, specific and quick. Reviewers look for bugs, clarity, security and tests, and they separate must-fix from nice-to-have. Automation helps: the pipeline runs tests on every PR, and branch protection rules on `main` can require a passing pipeline and at least one approval before merging. That is how a review step becomes a safe gate in DevSecOps, not a suggestion.

Never commit passwords, API keys or private keys. Once pushed, a secret is in the history even if you delete the file later, and you must treat it as leaked and replace it. Use a `.gitignore` for files like `.env`, and consider a secret scanner in your pipeline.
Your task

items: Create a practice repository, make a feature branch, commit twice and rebase it on a newer `main`.
Use `git stash` to switch branches in the middle of a change and come back.
Make a commit with a mistake, push it to a branch and fix it with `git revert`.
Create a tag `v0.1.0` and write one sentence on how you would roll back to it.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: `git log --oneline --graph` shows the history you expect after the rebase.
You can explain when to use revert and when to use reset.
You can name the strategy your own team or project uses, and why.

steps.say: You do the work on a short-lived branch.
You open a pull request. Tests run and a teammate reviews it.
After approval, it merges into main, which stays deployable.
A tag marks the release commit, so you can deploy it, and roll back to an earlier tag.

faqs.q: Should I use merge or rebase?
faqs.a: Use rebase to keep your own private branch up to date, and merge or squash-merge when the pull request is accepted. Never rebase commits that others have already pulled.

faqs.q: What is the difference between git revert and git reset?
faqs.a: Revert adds a new commit that undoes an earlier one and is safe on shared branches. Reset moves the branch pointer back and can erase history, so use it only on your own unshared work.

faqs.q: What should I do if I committed a secret?
faqs.a: Treat it as leaked: revoke or rotate the secret straight away, then remove it from the code. Deleting the file in a later commit does not remove it from history.

quiz.q: Which command safely undoes a commit that is already shared?
What is the golden rule of rebase?
options: Never rebase commits that others have already pulled

quiz.q: What is a Git tag commonly used for?
options: Marking a release such as v1.4.0

lessons.title: GitHub Actions: Your First CI Pipeline
lessons.metaTitle: GitHub Actions: Your First CI Pipeline
lessons.description: Build a CI pipeline with GitHub Actions that tests and builds a Node project on every push and pull request, using a matrix, caching and artifacts.

content.text: GitHub Actions is the automation service built into GitHub. When something happens in your repository, for example a push or a pull request, it starts a virtual machine, checks out your code and runs the steps you describe in a YAML file. It is a very good first CI tool, because it needs no server of your own, and the ideas you learn here (triggers, jobs, steps, secrets, artifacts) carry over to Jenkins, GitLab CI and the others. In this lesson you build a pipeline for a small Node project.
The vocabulary

items: **Workflow:** one YAML file in `.github/workflows/`. A repository can have many.
**Trigger (`on`):** the event that starts it, such as `push`, `pull_request`, a schedule or a manual button.
**Job:** a group of steps that runs on one fresh machine (a runner). Jobs run in parallel unless you say one `needs` another.
**Step:** one command (`run`) or one reusable action (`uses`).
**Action:** a ready-made step from the marketplace, for example `actions/checkout`.
**Runner:** the virtual machine, such as `ubuntu-latest`.

content.text: The sample project

The project is tiny on purpose: one function, two tests that use Node’s own test runner, and a build script. It was run in the course lab with Node 22: `npm ci` installed with zero packages, `npm test` passed both tests, and `npm run build` printed build finished. The lock file `package-lock.json` is part of the project, because `npm ci` needs it for repeatable installs.
export const sum = (a, b) => a + b;
The workflow file

Save this as `.github/workflows/ci.yml`. The file was checked by parsing the YAML and reading back its triggers, matrix and steps. It was not executed on GitHub for this course, because that needs a real repository, so the first run on your own repository is your final test.

name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    strategy:
      matrix:
        node: [20, 22]
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: ${{ matrix.node }}
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm test
      - run: npm run build
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        if: matrix.node == 22
        with:
          name: dist
          path: dist/
Reading it line by line

items: `on` starts the workflow for pushes to `main` and for pull requests that target `main`.
`strategy.matrix.node` runs the job twice, once with Node 20 and once with Node 22. A matrix is how you test against several versions without copying the job.
`actions/checkout@v4` downloads your code onto the runner. Without it the machine is empty.
`actions/setup-node@v4` installs Node and, with `cache: npm`, keeps downloaded packages between runs to save time.
`npm ci` installs exactly what the lock file says. It is faster and stricter than `npm install`, and it is what CI should use.
`npm test` and `npm run build` are your checks. If any step exits with a failure code, the job stops and turns red.
`upload-artifact` saves the build output so you can download it or use it in a later job. The `if` limits it to one matrix run.

content.text: Pin actions to a version, as in `@v4`, and review third-party actions before you use them. An action runs with access to your repository, so only use ones from sources you trust. For higher safety, teams pin to a full commit hash.
Make the pipeline matter

items: Push the project and the workflow to a GitHub repository, and open the Actions tab to watch the first run.
Break a test on purpose in a branch, open a pull request and watch the check fail.
In the repository settings, add a branch protection rule on `main` that requires this check to pass before merging. Now the pipeline is a real gate.
Fix the test and see the check turn green.

content.text: Secrets

Pipelines often need passwords or tokens, for example to deploy. Store them in the repository settings under Secrets, and read them in the workflow as `${{ secrets.NAME }}`. GitHub hides their values in logs. Never write them into the YAML file, and give each secret only the access it needs. For deployments to a cloud, a better practice you will meet later is OpenID Connect, which lets the workflow get short-lived access without a stored long-lived key.
Next steps

Later lessons add more to this pipeline: building a Docker image, scanning it for vulnerabilities, deploying to a server or Kubernetes, and sending notifications. The pattern stays the same, only more steps. Start small and add one thing at a time, running it after each addition.
Your task

items: Create a repository with the sample project and the workflow, and get a green run.
Add a failing test on a branch, open a pull request and confirm the check blocks it, with branch protection on.
Add a third Node version to the matrix.
Add a step that prints `node --version` and find it in the log.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: The Actions tab shows a green check for both matrix jobs.
A pull request with a failing test cannot be merged when branch protection is on.
You can say what `npm ci` does differently from `npm install`.

steps.say: A push or a pull request matches the on section of the workflow.
GitHub starts a fresh virtual machine, called a runner, for each job in the matrix.
The steps run in order: checkout, setup Node, npm ci, test, build. A failing step stops the job.
The result shows as a check on the commit or pull request. Branch protection can require it to be green.

faqs.q: Is GitHub Actions free?
faqs.a: GitHub offers a free allowance of minutes for many accounts, with different limits for public and private repositories, and the terms change. Check the current pricing page before you rely on it.

faqs.q: Why use npm ci instead of npm install in CI?
faqs.a: npm ci installs exactly the versions in the lock file and fails if the lock file and package.json disagree. This makes builds repeatable.

faqs.q: Can I run a workflow by hand?
faqs.a: Yes. Add workflow_dispatch to the on section and a Run workflow button appears in the Actions tab.

quiz.q: Where are GitHub Actions workflow files stored?
Why use npm ci in a pipeline?
options: It is the only way to run tests
It installs exactly what the lock file says, so builds are repeatable

quiz.q: How do you make a pipeline check a real gate for merging?
options: Add a branch protection rule that requires the check to pass

lessons.title: Cloud Computing Fundamentals: Public, Private, Hybrid, IaaS, PaaS and SaaS
lessons.description: Understand cloud computing, its benefits, public, private, hybrid and multi-cloud, IaaS, PaaS and SaaS, virtual machines and containers.

content.text: Before cloud computing, a company that wanted a website bought servers, put them in a room, connected cables, installed software and hired people to look after the machines. If the website became popular, the servers ran out of power, and ordering new ones took weeks. If it did not, the servers sat idle and the money was wasted. Cloud computing changes this: you rent computing power, storage and services over the internet from a provider, create them in minutes, and stop paying when you delete them.
What cloud computing is

Cloud computing means using computing resources, such as servers, storage, databases, networks and software, that belong to a provider and are delivered over the internet, usually paid for by use. The provider owns and runs the buildings (data centres), the hardware and the basic software. You choose what you want and how much, with a web console, a command line or code.
Benefits

items: **Speed:** a server in minutes instead of weeks.
**Pay for what you use:** no big purchase up front. You pay for the time and the amount, though a badly managed account can still become expensive.
**Scale up and down:** add capacity for a busy day and remove it after.
**Reach:** run your service in many countries without building a data centre in each.
**Managed services:** the provider takes care of patches, backups and hardware for things like databases, so your team spends time on its own product.
**Reliability tools:** copies in several places, if you design for them.

content.text: Cloud is not automatically cheaper or safer. A small steady workload can cost more in the cloud than on a rented server, and a wrong setting can expose data. The benefit comes from using it well. Later lessons show how to control cost and security.
Cloud deployment models

items: **Public cloud:** services are run by a provider such as AWS, Azure or Google Cloud and shared between many customers, with strong separation between them. It is the most common model.
**Private cloud:** the infrastructure is used by one organisation only, in its own data centre or hosted for it. It gives more control, and the organisation carries more of the work and cost.
**Hybrid cloud:** a mix of private systems and public cloud, joined together. A bank may keep sensitive records in its own data centre and use the public cloud for websites.

**Multi-cloud:** using more than one public cloud provider, to avoid depending on one, to use the best service of each, or because of company mergers. It adds complexity, so do not choose it only because it sounds safer.

content.text: IaaS, PaaS and SaaS

The three service models are about how much the provider manages for you. A pizza comparison is popular because it works. Making pizza at home means you do everything. Buying a frozen pizza means someone else made it and you bake it. Ordering a delivery means you only eat.

items: **IaaS, Infrastructure as a Service:** you rent the basic building blocks: virtual machines, disks and networks. You install and manage the operating system and everything above it. Examples: AWS EC2, Azure Virtual Machines, Google Compute Engine. Most control, most work.

**PaaS, Platform as a Service:** the provider also manages the operating system and runtime. You bring your code and settings. Examples: AWS Elastic Beanstalk, Azure App Service, Google App Engine and Cloud Run. Less control, less work.
**SaaS, Software as a Service:** a finished application that you use through a browser or app: Gmail, Google Docs, Microsoft 365, Slack. You manage only your data and users.

content.text: Between these, you will also hear FaaS, Function as a Service, or serverless functions such as AWS Lambda, where you upload a function and the provider runs it only when something calls it. The name serverless does not mean there are no servers. It means you do not manage them.
Virtualization, virtual machines and containers

Cloud providers run many customers on the same physical machines. They can do this safely because of virtualization: software called a hypervisor divides one physical machine into several virtual machines (VMs). Each VM has its own operating system, memory and disk, and cannot see the others. A VM behaves like a real computer, and takes about a minute to start.

Containers are lighter. Instead of a whole operating system for each one, containers share the host’s kernel and are separated by features of Linux. A container holds your application and what it needs, starts in a second or less, and uses much less memory. You will learn containers in depth in the Docker lessons. In short: a VM virtualizes the hardware, and a container virtualizes the operating system. Many systems use both: containers running inside VMs.
Your task

items: List five cloud services you already use in daily life and say whether each is IaaS, PaaS or SaaS.
Explain to a friend, without technical words, why a company would rent servers instead of buying them.
Choose a small website idea and write which model (IaaS, PaaS or functions) you would try first and why.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: You can explain IaaS, PaaS and SaaS using an example of each.
You can say the difference between hybrid and multi-cloud.
You can say how a container differs from a virtual machine in one sentence.

steps.say: IaaS gives you virtual machines. You install and look after the operating system and everything on it.
With PaaS the provider also looks after the operating system and runtime. You manage your code and settings.
With functions you only upload a piece of code. It runs when called and you pay for the run.
SaaS is a finished product. You use it and manage only your data and users.

faqs.q: Is cloud always cheaper than my own servers?
faqs.a: No. It can be cheaper for variable workloads and for small teams, and more expensive for steady heavy workloads or when it is poorly managed. Calculate for your own case, and set budget alerts.

faqs.q: Is serverless really without servers?
faqs.a: No. Servers still exist, but the provider manages them. You do not provision, patch or scale them yourself.

faqs.q: Do I need to use multi-cloud?
faqs.a: Most teams do not. It adds cost and complexity. Consider it when you have a clear reason such as legal rules, a specific service or a business agreement.

quiz.q: Which model gives you virtual machines that you manage from the operating system up?
What is hybrid cloud?
options: A mix of private systems and public cloud, joined together

quiz.q: How is a container different from a virtual machine?
options: Containers share the host kernel; a VM has its own operating system
A VM shares the host kernel

lessons.title: Regions, Availability Zones, High Availability, Cloud Pricing and Shared Responsibility
lessons.metaTitle: Cloud Regions, HA, Pricing and Security
lessons.description: Learn regions and availability zones, scaling, high availability, disaster recovery, cloud pricing models and the shared responsibility model.

content.text: Cloud providers sell reliability, but they do not give it automatically. You get it by building your system in the right way across the right places, and you pay for it. This lesson explains the vocabulary that every cloud course and interview uses: regions and zones, scaling, high availability, fault tolerance and disaster recovery, how cloud prices work, and the shared responsibility model that says who is in charge of security. The words are the same in AWS, Azure and Google Cloud, although the product names differ.
Regions and availability zones

items: A **region** is a geographic area where the provider has data centres, for example Mumbai, London, Montreal or Cape Town. You choose a region for each resource. Pick one near your users to reduce delay, and check the law: some data must stay in a particular country. Prices and the list of services also differ by region.

An **availability zone (AZ)** is one or more separate data centres inside a region, with their own power, cooling and network. Zones are close enough to talk fast and far enough that a fire or power cut in one does not take the others. Azure and Google Cloud use the same idea with their own names.

content.text: The usual pattern for a reliable application is to run copies in at least two zones of one region. If one zone fails, the others keep going. Not every region has the same number of zones, and the exact count changes, so look at your provider’s page when you plan.
Scalability and elasticity

items: **Scalability** is the ability to handle more load. **Vertical scaling** means a bigger machine (more CPU and memory). It is simple, but has a limit, and often needs a restart. **Horizontal scaling** means more machines of the same size behind a load balancer. It has no real limit and is the usual cloud approach, but your application must work with several copies at once, which means keeping session data and files outside the individual server.
**Elasticity** is scaling automatically, up when load rises and down when it falls, so you do not pay for idle machines. Auto scaling groups and Kubernetes autoscalers do this.

content.text: High availability, fault tolerance and disaster recovery

items: **High availability (HA)** means the service stays up despite failures, with only a short interruption at most. You get it by removing single points of failure: two or more copies, in different zones, behind a load balancer, with health checks.
**Fault tolerance** goes further: the system continues without any visible interruption when a part fails. It is more expensive, because it needs full spare capacity running all the time.
**Disaster recovery (DR)** is the plan for a big failure, for example a whole region lost, a bad deployment that damages data, or an attack. It relies on backups and a way to rebuild elsewhere.

content.text: Two numbers define a DR plan, and you will hear them in interviews. **RPO, recovery point objective,** is how much data you can afford to lose, measured as time: with an RPO of one hour, you need a backup at least hourly. **RTO, recovery time objective,** is how long you can afford to be down. Lower numbers cost more. Typical strategies, from cheapest and slowest to dearest and fastest, are backup and restore, pilot light (a small core always running), warm standby (a scaled-down full copy) and active-active (full copies in several regions serving users all the time).
A backup that has never been restored is not proof of anything. Schedule a practice restore, write down how long it took, and use that as your honest RTO.
How cloud pricing works

items: **Pay-as-you-go (on demand):** you pay for what you use, by the second, minute or hour, with no commitment. It is the most flexible and the most expensive per unit.
**Commitments:** you promise to use a certain amount for a year or three in return for a lower price. AWS calls them Savings Plans and Reserved Instances. Azure and Google Cloud have similar offers.
**Spot or preemptible capacity:** spare capacity at a big discount, which the provider can take back at short notice. Good for jobs that can be interrupted.
**Free tiers and credits:** most providers give a small free allowance or trial credit for new accounts. Terms change often, so read the current offer.

content.text: Bills usually have several parts: compute time, storage, requests, and data transfer. Data leaving the provider to the internet is charged, while data coming in is often free. Surprises tend to come from things left running, large data transfers, idle but paid resources (such as unattached disks and public addresses) and logs that grow without limit. Protect yourself with a budget alert on day one, tags that show which project owns each resource, and a habit of deleting practice resources when you finish.
The shared responsibility model

When you use the cloud, security is shared. The provider is responsible for security of the cloud: the buildings, the hardware, the network and the virtualization layer. You are responsible for security in the cloud: your data, your accounts and permissions, your network rules, the operating system on a VM you manage, and your application code. How much falls on you depends on the model. With IaaS, you patch the operating system. With a managed database, the provider patches it, but you still decide who can connect to it and which data it holds.

items: Most cloud data leaks come from the customer side: a storage bucket left public, an access key committed to Git, a database open to the whole internet, or a powerful account without multi-factor authentication.
Protect the root or owner account with MFA, give people individual accounts, and grant only the access they need.
Turn on logging of who did what, so you can investigate.

content.text: Your task

items: Pick a cloud provider and find the list of its regions. Note which is nearest to you, and how many zones it has.
Draw a web application that survives the loss of one zone: load balancer, two app servers, a database with a standby.
Write an RPO and RTO for a service you know, and say which DR strategy would fit.
Find the current free tier terms for one provider, and write down what would still cost money.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: You can explain the difference between a region and an availability zone.
You can explain RPO and RTO with an example.
You can name three things that are always the customer’s responsibility in the cloud.

steps.say: A load balancer spreads visitors over copies of the app in more than one availability zone.
Zone A runs one copy of the app, with its own power and network.
Zone B runs a second copy. If Zone A fails, the load balancer keeps using Zone B.
The database keeps a standby in the other zone, so data survives too. Backups protect against bigger disasters.

faqs.q: What is the difference between high availability and disaster recovery?
faqs.a: High availability keeps a service running through small failures such as one server or zone. Disaster recovery is the plan to restore the service after a large failure, such as a lost region or damaged data.

faqs.q: Why is data transfer a common surprise on bills?
faqs.a: Data leaving the provider to the internet, and sometimes between regions, is charged per amount. Large downloads and busy sites can cost a lot more than the servers do.

faqs.q: Who is responsible if my storage bucket is public?
faqs.a: You are. The provider secures the platform, but how you configure your own resources and permissions is your responsibility under the shared responsibility model.

quiz.q: What is an availability zone?
options: One or more separate data centres inside a region

quiz.q: What does RPO mean?
options: How long you can be down
How much data you can afford to lose, measured as time

quiz.q: Who is responsible for making sure your storage bucket is not public?
